To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the amount of feed intake prior to feed deprivation is important in determining how long it takes for cattle to resume eating after a period of feed deprivation.
prefast feed intake influences the ability of steers to adapt to feed and water deprivation.
an increase in the prefast feed intake resulted in a shorter post-fast adaptation period.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of prefast feed and water intake on subsequent feed and water deprivation and realimentation.
the influence of feed restriction on rumen microbial populations and their activity, and the influence of feed intake on the recovery of the animal from a fast.
the effects of prefast feed level on the response to a subsequent fast in beef steers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prefast feed intake of 1.75 to 2% of body weight was optimum for the recovery of steers after 48-h fasts.
the greater the prefast intake of energy, water, and electrolytes, the shorter the recovery time after fasting.
prefast feed intake influences the rate of postfast realimentation feed and water consumption.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
prefast feed intake is a major determinant of the extent and duration of postfast adaptation.
prefast feed intake influences the rate of postfast recovery from feed deprivation.
a high prefast feed intake would result in a greater recovery from feed and/or water deprivation than a low intake.
The main takeaway from our work is that
if you want to fast your steer or heifer for a show or sale, you should be sure to feed them a high quality diet for at least 7 to 10 days before the fast.
the more an animal eats, the more it can eat when it is not eating.
if we are going to fast animals, we should do it in a way that minimizes stress, and that means providing a high quality diet in the days prior to fasting.
